Recently, however, labor's efforts as well as those of consumer, governmental and other groups have been thwarted by anti-competitive practices of state [...] instances, the Federal Trade Commission (FTC), a watch-dog consumer agency of the federal government, intervened and used its statutory authority to stop such activities through [...] In the closing days of the 97th Congress, special-interest lobbies led by the American Medical Association (AMA) tried to eliminate the consumer protection, anti-monopoly powers of the FTC in the area of professional services. In essence, the AMA sought to carve out for itself and certain other professions a special antitrust immunity. During House debate on a bill to provide funding for the FTC, Rep. Tom Luken (D-Ohio) offered an AMA-sponsored amendment to prevent the FTC from intervening to stop monopolistic practices in the health care marketplace. In a strategy designed to sidetrack the Luken amendment, the AFL-CIO joined consumer groups in backing a bipartisan, compromise substitute amendment by Reps. Jim Florio (D-N.J.) and John Dingell (D-Mich.) which essentially retained the FTC's jurisdiction. This strategy failed, however, when the House rejected the substitute amendment 195-208 on Dec. 4, after which the House agreed to the Luken proposal. (Fortunately, the Senate rejected a similar amendment - see Senate Vote 4 - so this anti-consumer proposal did not become law.) For substitute - Right. Against substitute - Wrong.

corrections: date 1982-12-04 -> 1982-12-01 per Voteview roll 732 (4 Dec was a Saturday with no House roll calls)
aflcio_description: The defeat of the Dingell/Florio amendment (House Vote 2) paved the way for approval of the Luken amendment to eliminate the FTC's consumer protection authority in this area. As passed by the House, the Luken amendment gave the AMA the anti-trust exemption it sought. By a 245-155 vote the House approved the Luken amendment on Dec. 4. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

Very few public works projects are approved by Congress without first facing right-wing attempts to remove the protections of a key federal fair wage law - the Davis-Bacon Act. This 1931 law ensures that workers on federally financed construction projects will be paid at the wage rates that prevail in their area of the country. For 50 years the Davis-Bacon Act has guaranteed that local contractors who uphold community labor standards will not be undercut by out-of-state firms using cut-rate labor. There were three anti-Davis-Bacon amendments offered to the highway repair/job creation legislation of the 1982 lame-duck session. The most serious threat was an amendment by Rep. Buddy Roemer (D-La.) to restrict the Davis-Bacon requirements to "initial construction" projects in the highway bill. This amendment could have removed Davis-Bacon protections from all highway resurfacing and repair work under the bill. Fortunately, the House rejected the Roemer amendment 191-194 on Dec. 6. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

National unemployment in 1982 climbed to the highest level since the Great Depression. By year's end more than 11 million workers were officially counted as jobless. Yet as additional hundreds of thousands of American families suffered layoffs and joined the ranks of the "new poor," President Reagan urged patience. By the fall elections, the patience of the voters had worn thin, and many Congressional adherents of "stay the course" - known as "Reagan robots" - were defeated. The message from the electorate was clear: Change course, take action now to reverse the decline in the economy. Congress returned to Washington for the post-election, lame-duck session with Democrats and Republicans alike declaring that creating jobs would be their Number 1 priority. House Democrats crafted a $5.4 billion job-creation program designed to swiftly put the unemployed back to work on a wide variety of programs, including sewer and waste disposal, flood prevention, veterans' hospital modernization, parks, public housing maintenance, and prison and jail repair. "Do nothing" Republicans tried to kill even this modest job-creation program. Their efforts were in vain as a motion by Rep. Silvio Conte (R-Mass.) to send the bill back to committee to kill the job-creation package was defeated 191-215 on Dec. 14. (Ultimately, however, the job-creation package was killed by the threat of a veto by President Reagan.) Against recommital - Right. For recommital - Wrong.

bill_title: Creating Jobs for the Unemployed I
aflcio_description: Although unemployment was the number one issue in the 1982 elections, efforts by congressional Democrats to pass job-creation legislation were thwarted by Republicans in the Senate and by the repeated threat of veto by President Reagan. Despite this opposition, the House passed a $5.4 billion job-creation package of proven public works projects (See House Vote 5). In the Senate, Minority Leader Robert Byrd (D-W.Va.) offered a similar package of jobs programs as an amendment to the highway repair bill. The Byrd amendment provided that the job-creating work would be financed by "capping" the planned 1983 income tax cuts for high-income individuals - a measure long advocated by the AFL-CIO. The tax cut would be delayed only for those with incomes greater than $50,000 per year. The Byrd amendment also included an extension of unemployment benefits. As a package, the Byrd amendment combined a concern for the 12 million unemployed Americans with a commitment to fairness in tax policy. Unfortunately, Republican opposition killed this initiative as the Byrd amendment was defeated 44-53 on Dec. 14. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

bill_title: Restoring Jobs in America's Auto Industry
corrections: description: the card sets 'During that same period. Japanese auto imports jumped'; the store had normalised that period to a comma. Restored 31 Aug 2026 and pinned in audit_1982.CARD_TYPOS
aflcio_description: The flood of foreign imports into the United States has contributed to the decline of major domestic industries over the last decade. For example, in the auto industry and its many supplier industries - steel, rubber, glass, textiles and electronics - 750,000 jobs were lost between 1978 and 1981. During that same period, Japanese auto imports jumped by more than 33 percent while domestic auto sales plummeted by the same amount. To help put America back to work and restore the health of this key industry, the AFL-CIO urged Congress to adopt legislation to require foreign auto manufacturers with a large share of the U.S. market to manufacture increasing portions of their vehicles here, using American labor and materials. Called the domestic content bill, the legislation would produce an estimated 800,000 jobs in auto production and supplier industries. By the closing days of the 97th Congress, after an intensive labor lobbying effort, a majority of House members had agreed to cosponsor the domestic content bill. On Dec. 15 the content bill was passed by a 215-188 vote. Although a similar bill failed to reach the Senate floor for a vote, the record of committee hearings and the strong House vote were expected to encourage action on the content bill in the new 98th Congress. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

bill_title: "Buy American" Protection to Save U.S. Jobs
aflcio_description: Long-overdue legislation to rehabilitate the nation's highways was passed in the lame-duck session to provide badly needed maintenance of the U.S. transportation network while giving some measure of relief to the unemployed by putting an estimated 320,000 Americans back to work. During Senate debate, Sen. Howard Metzenbaum (D-Ohio) tried to create even more jobs by offering an amendment to the bill requiring that only U.S.-made steel and cement be used in projects funded by the bill. This would ensure the greatest amount of "ripple effect" in creating jobs in supplier industries for this highway program. Once again, Republicans thwarted this job-creating effort. Sens. John Chafee (R-R.I.) and John Danforth (R-Mo.) filibustered the Metzenbaum amendment after which Sen. Howard Baker (R-Tenn.) offered a motion to table it. Over labor's objections, the Senate approved the Baker motion by a 51-47 vote on Dec. 15. (However, a "buy American" provision which had been approved earlier by the House was maintained in the bill as signed into law.) Against tabling - Right. For tabling - Wrong.

bill_title: Protecting Consumers by Containing Health Care Costs
corrections: description: the card sets 'special-interest lobbies', as the House half (House S2) does; the store had 'special interest'. Both halves break the compound at the line, and specialinterest is not a word, so the hyphen is a compound hyphen. Restored 31 Aug 2026
aflcio_description: In the closing days of the 97th Congress, special-interest lobbies led by the American Medical Association (AMA) tried to eliminate the consumer protection, anti-monopoly powers of the FTC in the area of professional services. In essence, the AMA sought to carve out for itself and certain other professions a special anti-trust immunity. In the health care field this proposal would allow medical associations to thwart efforts by unions and other groups to lower health care costs for their members. After the battle was lost in the House (see House Votes 2 and 3), the Senate turned the tables on the AMA. During debate on an appropriations bill, the Senate approved a motion by Sen. Warren Rudman (R-N.H.) to table and thereby kill an amendment by Sen. James McClure (R-Ida.) to bar use of FTC funds to combat monopolistic practices by the professions. The tabling motion passed 59-37 on Dec. 16. For tabling - Right. Against tabling - Wrong.

bill_title: Maintaining Federal Employee Health Care Protections
corrections: description: the card sets 'the Reagan reductions, are finding'; the store had dropped that comma. Restored 31 Aug 2026
aflcio_description: Federal employees have undergone more than their share of misery caused by Reagan budget cuts. Early in his Administration, the President declared that his goal was to cut the federal work force by 75,000 workers. Those federal employees who survive the Reagan reductions, are finding that the Administration is determined to raise premiums and reduce coverage under their health care plans. Congressional conservatives, taking their cue from the Administration, repeatedly tried to eliminate abortion coverage now available under federal health insurance policies, for which federal workers pay 60 percent of the premium. While the AFL-CIO has taken no position on the issue of abortion, to the federation the key issue is not abortion but whether Congress can disregard the limited collective bargaining rights of federal workers by arbitrarily removing certain health benefits that are now available to workers in the private sector. During the lame-duck session a continuing appropriations bill contained language to eliminate this health care coverage. However, during final debate a labor-backed committee amendment to remove the harmful language was approved 49-48 on Dec. 16. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

bill_title: Creating Jobs for the Unemployed II
aflcio_description: After Sen. Robert Byrd's (D-W.Va.) package of job-creating programs failed to achieve passage (See Senate Vote 2), Democrats and some Republicans worked to attach a smaller, $1.2-billion public works package to the continuing appropriations bill that Congress needed to pass before adjournment. This modest attempt to create jobs in the face of massive unemployment had bipartisan support. A key vote came on an amendment by Sen. Pete Domenici (R-N.M.) to delete the job-creation programs from the resolution. The Domenici amendment failed 46-50 on Dec. 16. (However, with President Reagan threatening to veto the vital continuing appropriations resolution if it included any jobs programs, House and Senate conferees decided to delete the job-creating public works provision from the resolution in order to avert a wasteful shutdown of most government agencies.) Against - Right. For - Wrong.

bill_title: Stopping the Export of U.S. Jobs
aflcio_description: The Reagan Administration's so-called Caribbean Basin Initiative, strongly backed by big business, contained special trade privileges for this region that would encourage U.S.-based multinationals to close their domestic plants and build new plants abroad in order to funnel their products through the Caribbean. The AFL-CIO warned Congress that this misguided proposal would do little to improve industry or working conditions in the Caribbean. Rather it would accelerate the flood of imports into the United States and export thousands of American jobs at a time of record high unemployment. Earlier, the federation reiterated its commitment to Caribbean workers and supported congressional passage of an economic aid program to help the region meet its massive problems and develop its economy. Despite labor's opposition, the House passed the job-destroying Caribbean Basin bill by a 260-142 vote on Dec. 17. (The Senate, however, failed to bring the measure to a vote, so the Caribbean bill did not become law.) For - Wrong. Against - Right.

corrections: date 1982-12-19 -> 1982-12-18 per Voteview roll 954 (19 Dec was a Sunday with no Senate roll calls)
aflcio_description: Davis-Bacon prevailing wage provisions of the highway rehabilitation legislation underwent attack in both the House and Senate, as conservatives attempted to remove assurances that workers on federally contracted construction projects will be paid the wages prevailing in their area of the country (See House Vote 4). In the Senate, Don Nickles (R-Okla.) offered an amendment to delete provisions specifying that Davis-Bacon protections would apply to major interstate highway repairs, as well as new construction. At the urging of organized labor, Sen. Robert Stafford (R-Vt.) moved to table, and thereby kill, the Nickles anti-labor amendment. By a 48-46 vote on Dec. 19, the Senate approved the Stafford motion. For tabling - Right. Against tabling - Wrong.

bill_title: Creating Jobs - Restoring Highways and Transit
aflcio_description: Labor's hopes for passage of major job-creating legislation in the post-election lame-duck session were thwarted by "do nothing" Republicans led by a President committed to "staying the course" instead of putting America back to work. One casualty was a broad-based package of job-creating public works programs approved by the House and Senate only to be dropped in conference after being threatened with a Presidential veto. Even the highway repair bill, which most observers expected to sail through Congress, was delayed by a stubborn right-wing Republican filibuster in the Senate. Eventually the Senate voted to stop the filibuster and passed the AFL-CIO-backed highway measure by a 56-34 vote on Dec. 20. As enacted, the highway bill will create an estimated 320,000 jobs in the repair and maintenance of interstate and other highways and improvements to mass transit systems. It will also help save thousands of lives by rehabilitating some of the most dangerous stretches of our nation's highways. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

bill_title: Jobs I: Public Works Job Creation and Recession Relief
aflcio_description: With the nation in the depths of the worst postwar recession, Congress in March passed a $4.9 billion job-creation and humanitarian aid bill. This was the only anti-recession bill to survive the threat of a Reagan veto and a Republican-dominated Senate. It included funds for a variety of job-creating projects including highway and mass transit improvements, repair of schools, veterans' hospitals and other public buildings, water and sewer improvements, weatherization of homes, day care, Head Start and other social services, and special jobs programs for youths and the elderly. The legislation provides for temporary employment of nearly one million Americans. A key vote came on a motion by Rep. Silvio Conte (R-Mass.) to recommit the bill to committee in order to cut funding for construction projects by $423 million. The AFL-CIO, urging Congress to approve the strongest possible jobs package, worked to defeat the Conte motion, which was rejected 158-256 on Mar. 3. For recommittal - Wrong. Against recommittal - Right.

Early in 1983 Congress passed a package of amendments to Social Security designed to improve the long-term health of the nation's No. 1 retirement plan. Most of the changes had been recommended by a bipartisan commission that included AFL-CIO President Lane Kirkland. The commission proposal was later packaged in an omnibus Social Security bill and sent to the House floor. During debate conservative Republicans and "boll weevil" Democrats succeeded in a major future weakening of the program. Rep. Jake Pickle (D-Tex.) offered an amendment to raise the retirement age from 65 to 67, starting in the year 2009 and phasing in by 2027. All workers who are now younger than 40 would be adversely affected by the amendment. It also increased from 20 percent to 30 percent the benefit reduction penalty for those retiring before age 67. Progressive Democrats backed by the AFL-CIO countered with an alternative amendment offered by Rep. Claude Pepper. But the House rejected the alternative and approved the Pickle amendment by a 228-202 vote on Mar. 9. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

bill_title: Jobs I: Creating New Jobs and Providing Recession Relief
corrections: tally printed prevailing-side-first as 53-34; the roll call is 34-53 on the Levin amendment per Voteview roll 16
aflcio_description: During consideration of the only job-creation bill passed by Congress during the Reagan recession, Sen. Carl Levin (D-Mich.) made an attempt to increase the scope of the program to provide more meaningful relief to the 13.2 million Americans suffering from joblessness. Levin's amendment would have added $1.6 billion in funds for community jobs programs and recession relief such as health care, food and emergency shelter for the homeless. But a majority in the GOP-controlled Senate turned their backs on the unemployed and voted 53-34 on Mar. 11 to reject the Levin amendment. At a time of depression-level unemployment, Republicans argued that the cost was too great even though it amounted to only $126 in job-creation funds for each unemployed American. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

Conservatives who have long sought to weaken the social security program finally got their chance under Ronald Reagan in 1983. Taking advantage of the need to stabilize the financing of social security, conservatives pushed through an increase in the retirement age for full social security benefits from 65 to 66. This step backward was coupled with another regressive provision imposing a 30 percent benefit reduction penalty for those who must retire before age 66. The AFL-CIO strongly opposed these changes noting that many workers who retire before age 65 do so for reasons of poor health. Unable to defeat this provision, Sen. Bill Bradley (D-N.J.) offered a compromise amendment to provide for improved disability benefits for those who are unable to work until age 66. Again conservatives led the charge against the Bradley amendment, which was rejected 30-61 on Mar. 21. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

Searching for ways to reduce President Reagan's monstrous $200-billion-per-year budget deficits, Congress in 1982 enacted a tax reform to require that taxes on sizeable stock dividends and savings account interest payments be withheld at time of payment. This so-called withholding tax reform was not a tax increase, but only a better means of collecting taxes that were due but were going unpaid. The reform would raise $13 billion in three years by stopping tax-cheating. The AFL-CIO, noting that taxes are withheld from workers' paychecks, saw no reason why taxes should not be withheld from unearned income, and had long advocated enactment of this tax reform. In 1983 the banking lobby went on the offensive to repeal the tax withholding reform before it was scheduled to take effect. The key vote in the Senate came on an amendment by Sen. John Melcher (D-Mont.) to delay the tax reform for six months, opening the door toward eventual repeal. Sen. Daniel P. Moynihan (D-N.Y.) moved to kill the Melcher amendment, by tabling it, and succeeded by a 54-43 vote on Mar. 22. But the Congress, overwhelmed by the bankers' postcard lobbying blitz, later repealed the tax withholding reform. For tabling - Right. Against tabling - Wrong.

In 1981 and to a lesser extent in 1982, Congressional Republicans joined by "boll weevil" Democrats approved federal budgets with drastic cuts in programs for working people and the poor along with tax cuts for the wealthy. After the 1982 elections, however, Congress viewed the results of the Reagan experiment and did not like what it saw: unemployment, soup lines and enormous budget deficits. In March 1983 the House approved an AFL-CIO-backed budget that began to restore funding of jobs, training, unemployment benefits, education, and other programs. This budget, while not as comprehensive as what the AFL-CIO had proposed, stopped the Reagan Administration slashing of programs and began the turnaround of budget priorities. The AFL-CIO-backed budget was approved 229-196 on Mar. 23. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

corrections: bill from the roll call's own Voteview description (S. Con. Res. 27); the bill_number field is empty
aflcio_description: Medical care costs have increased at three times the general rate of inflation over the last decade. The AFL-CIO has offered several proposals to limit profiteering by physicians and hospitals while guaranteeing health care coverage. The Reagan Administration, on the other hand, has pushed a "Robin Hood in reverse" health care program. The Reagan premise is that the more people have to pay for health care, the less they will use health care services. In 1981 the first Reagan budget cuts reduced Medicare funding by $3 billion over three years. Eighty percent of these cuts have been absorbed not by hospitals or doctors but by elderly patients. In 1983 the President asked for another $1.8 billion cut in Medicare. The Senate rejected this request but did pass an $800 million cut, thus forcing the elderly to reach deeper in their pockets to make up the difference. A key vote came on an amendment by Sen. Max Baucus (D-Mont.) to restore $400 million for Medicare. But a majority of Senators bought the Reagan program of making the sick pay for their misfortune, and rejected the Baucus amendment 45-50 on May 4. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

corrections: bill from the roll call's own Voteview description (S. Con. Res. 27); the bill_number field is empty
aflcio_description: One of the humanitarian recession-relief programs pushed by the AFL-CIO was health care benefits for the unemployed. When workers are jobless they usually lose health care insurance. Since most jobless workers are unable to pay for private insurance and are not eligible for Medicaid, they and their families must do without basic medical care. As unemployment hovered at 9 percent, the House was the first to approve a health care program (see House Vote 6). The Senate in its budget bill included a low level of funding for a watered-down program. Sen. Edward Kennedy (D-Mass.) tried to bring the Senate bill in line with the funding levels of the House version, but again Republicans balked. The Senate rejected Kennedy's amendment 36-63 on May 5. Later in the year, arch-conservatives led by Sen. Don Nickles (R-Okla.) stopped action even on a modest version of the health care bill. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

corrections: bill from the roll call's own Voteview description (S. Con. Res. 27); the bill_number field is empty
aflcio_description: President Reagan's budget cuts in federal aid to public schools have worsened education problems by forcing the cancellation of special teaching programs and by tightening the squeeze on local school districts. Many teaching posts are unfilled, particularly in math and the sciences, because school districts cannot afford to pay competitive salaries to their staffs. Meanwhile America's international competitors, such as Japan, attribute their successes to a firm commitment to education. During debate on the federal budget, Sen. Ernest Hollings (D-S.C.) offered an amendment to add $1.5 billion in education funds. This included $200 million for a new math and science program, as well as basic grants to elementary and secondary schools. The Hollings amendment also provided help for 600,000 additional needy students to meet tuition payments. Sen. Pete Domenici (R-N.M.), acting as President Reagan's point man, moved to kill the Hollings amendment. But supporters of education prevailed as Domenici's tabling motion failed 46-48 on May 5, paving the way for adoption of a compromise education funding amendment. For tabling - Wrong. Against tabling - Right.

With 9.4 million Americans out of work and fewer than 35 percent of them receiving unemployment benefits, the House passed a recession relief program of emergency loans to help unemployed homeowners avoid foreclosure and loss of their homes. The House-passed legislation was modest and well-crafted; it would authorize $760 million in emergency loans to jobless homeowners considered good risks to repay the loan when economic conditions improve and they find work again. This bill also provided emergency shelter for the homeless. The House passed the mortgage foreclosure relief bill 216-196 on May 11 despite opposition by the Reagan White House and House Republicans. The AFL-CIO continues to urge action in the Senate where conservative Republicans have stalled the measure. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

corrections: bill from the roll call's own Voteview description (S. Con. Res. 27); the bill_number field is empty
aflcio_description: In 1981 and 1982, President Reagan used the federal budget process to force big cuts in most programs while allowing huge tax cuts for the wealthy. But by 1983 the results of these policies - deep recession, double-digit unemployment and record budget deficits - were casting doubt on Reaganomics even among members of Congress who had voted for the Reagan program. In May 1983, debate about the economy focused on the new federal budget. The AFL-CIO urged that programs such as job-creation, education and training be restored and that tax loopholes be closed to get the budget under control. The President, however, refused to budge from his disastrous course. In the Senate, Majority Leader Howard Baker (R-Tenn.) and Budget Committee Chairman Pete Domenici (R-N.M.) offered a budget that essentially maintained Reaganomics by providing for a new round of program cuts with no room for tax reform such as the AFL-CIO-backed $700 tax cap (see Senate Vote 9). Sen. Lawton Chiles (D-Fla.) moved to kill this unfair budget and the Senate agreed 52-48 on May 12. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

Senate action on President Reagan's Caribbean Basin Initiative bill (see House Vote 2 for details) moved forward when the Senate Finance Committee packaged several bills, including CBI, with legislation that repealed a key 1982 tax compliance reform (see Senate Vote 8 for details). Sen. Russell Long (D-La.) offered a tabling motion to kill the entire labor-opposed package including CBI. But the President's conservative allies rallied to defeat the Long motion 46-51 on June 16. This vote paved the way for eventual enactment into law of the job-destroying CBI program. For tabling - Right. Against tabling - Wrong.

bill_title: Helping the Unemployed Avoid Mortgage Foreclosure and Eviction
aflcio_description: The Reagan recession brought with it not only the national misery of high unemployment but also soup lines, bankruptcies, foreclosures and evictions in record numbers. The AFL-CIO asked Congress to approve legislation that would provide emergency loans to unemployed homeowners threatened with foreclosure until economic conditions improved and the jobless could find work. Again, the Reagan White House opposed this temporary relief program. Over Republican opposition, the House passed a home mortgage foreclosure relief bill (see House Vote 13). In the Senate, Sen. Don Riegle (D-Mich.) and moderate Republican Sen. John Heinz (R-Pa.) offered a similar bill. Once again, Reagan-led conservatives blocked action and approved a tabling motion by Sen. Jake Garn (R-Utah) to kill the program. The vote was 55-39 on June 21. For tabling - Wrong. Against tabling - Right.

In 1981 Congress approved a three-year package of Reagan "supply side" tax cuts, ignoring the AFL-CIO's warning that the bill gave the bulk of its benefits to the wealthy. By 1983 the AFL-CIO's prediction came true. Working people had received a paltry $5 or $10 per week in Reagan tax cuts, an amount erased by higher state and local taxes. The wealthy, meanwhile, enjoyed huge windfalls. The President himself, with an income of $750,000 in 1982, received $91,619 that year in tax benefits from his own legislation. To restore an element of fairness, the AFL-CIO urged Congress to "cap" the 1983 tax savings at $720 per taxpayer, thus maintaining full tax cuts for families with incomes of $45,000 or less, but stopping the enormous windfalls for those who don't need extra tax cuts. The House passed this tax-fairness legislation 229-191 on June 23. Unfortunately, the Republican-controlled Senate later killed the bill. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

A major AFL-CIO initiative to restore an element of fairness to the Reagan supply-side tax program was legislation to impose a $700 "cap" on the 1983 tax cut (see House Vote 17 for details). The tax cap would retain the full tax break for wage earners earning $45,000 or less per year but limit the tax windfall for the rich to $700. It would also raise $6 billion in lost revenues at a time of record-high $200 billion budget deficits. The tax cap passed the House, but the Republican-controlled Senate, bowing to President Reagan's pressure, rejected it by a 45-55 vote on June 29. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

bill_title: Davis-Bacon: Fair Wages for Construction Workers
aflcio_description: The 1931 Davis-Bacon Act insures that workers on federally financed construction projects will be paid at wage rates that prevail in their area of the country. For over 50 years it has assured local contractors who uphold community labor standards a fair chance to compete for government projects without being undercut by outside firms using cut-rate labor. It has also protected the government and taxpayers from fly-by-night operators seeking to win federal contracts by paying wages too low to attract competent craftsmen. In 1983, House conservatives led by Rep. Robert Walker (R-Pa.) renewed their piecemeal attack on the law by trying to remove Davis-Bacon protections from local construction projects under the Economic Development Act. The Walker amendment was overwhelmingly rejected 148-270 on July 12. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

bill_title: Jobs II: Preventing Export of Jobs
aflcio_description: In 1983 the Reagan Administration once again pushed its so-called Caribbean Basin Initiative, a package of tax and trade privileges that would wipe out all tariffs and protections, thus stimulating Caribbean imports into the United States and further wiping out U.S. jobs. President Reagan claimed his bill was designed to boost the economies of friendly Caribbean nations. A close reading of the legislation, however, revealed that once again the Reagan Administration was pushing welfare for multinational corporations, not the needy workers of the Caribbean nations. For example, under the Reagan bill only 20 percent of a product need be made in a Caribbean nation, the remainder could come from factories elsewhere, including the Far East. All would be duty-free. The AFL-CIO endorsed an alternative bill designed to provide real help to Caribbean nations while preventing export of U.S. jobs. But the job-saving alternative did not receive consideration because 131 House Republicans, with the help of 81 Democrats, blocked its consideration by narrowly passing a debate rule that allowed only the Reagan bill to come to a vote, with no chance for job-saving amendments. The "closed" rule was approved by a 212-204 vote on July 13. For the rule - Wrong. Against the rule - Right.

corrections: tally 246-178 -> 171-255 per Voteview roll 299; the printed figure is record 3's tally and no 246-178 was cast on 3 Aug
aflcio_description: Most people receive their health insurance through their jobs. If they are laid off, they lose these benefits and usually find that they are not eligible for federal Medicaid assistance. The jobless and their families are then forced to do without health care or buy expensive private insurance at a time when their major source of income has been cut off. To remedy this, the AFL-CIO urged Congress to pass a program of humanitarian relief providing health care for the jobless. In August, the House approved a $4 billion health care bill to provide minimum family health insurance protection. The key vote came on a recommittal motion by Rep. Tom Tauke (R-Iowa) to gut the bill by removing most of its funding. The Tauke motion was rejected 246-178 on Aug. 3. The bill faces an uncertain future in the GOP-controlled Senate. For recommittal - Wrong. Against recommittal - Right.

bill_title: Trade Adjustment Benefits for the Unemployed
aflcio_description: In 1962 Congress created Trade Adjustment Assistance - a special program of unemployment compensation and job retraining assistance for those made jobless in industries hurt by imports. The 1981-82 Reagan Administration budget cuts nearly eliminated TAA. In 1983 Congress reversed gears and began to restore funding for the program. In September the House passed legislation to continue the TAA program through 1985. The bill added more funds for the program and extended its benefits to workers displaced in industries that supply the primary manufacturers. Conservatives led by Rep. Bill Frenzel (R-Minn.) tried to recommit the bill in order to cut funding and restrict eligibility for TAA benefits. Frenzel's motion was rejected 194-218 on Sept. 15. For recommittal - Wrong. Against recommittal - Right.

bill_title: Jobs III: Local Public Service Jobs
aflcio_description: As the Reagan recession continued to take its toll through the fall of 1983, the AFL-CIO continued to urge Congress to approve jobs legislation to help the 18.2 million unemployed or underemployed Americans. The House responded by passing a $3.5 billion jobs bill designed to improve community services such as health care and immunization, nutrition for the elderly and handicapped, emergency food and shelter for the unemployed and homeless, and day care for children of working parents. The bill sponsored by Rep. Gus Hawkins (D-Calif.) also includes funds for repair of public streets, bridges, public buildings, and water systems. Priority for jobs would go to those who had exhausted unemployment compensation. The community jobs bill was approved 246-178 on Sept. 21. The Republican controlled Senate has stalled this important employment relief measure. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

Federal revenue sharing, first enacted in 1972, provides grants to local governments for use on locally controlled programs, based on local priorities. These grants have been used in a wide variety of projects ranging from pothole repair on local streets to health screening and immunization. Revenue sharing has provided jobs and helped soften the blow of recession in many communities. In 1983 Congress passed a three-year extension of revenue sharing. The level of funding in the House version was $450 million higher than the Senate's. Sen. Bill Bradley (D-N.J.) offered an amendment to compromise by adding $225 million to the Senate bill, but with President Reagan staunchly opposed, conservative Senators closed their eyes to the hardship of recession and rejected the Bradley amendment 36-58 on Sept. 21. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

The Reagan recession caused the layoff of millions of Americans who had never been unemployed before; it also worsened the severity of their joblessness. The average duration of unemployment jumped from 13 weeks in January 1982 to 20 weeks in August 1983. Budget cuts in federal unemployment compensation left less than 35 percent of the currently unemployed receiving benefits. For many of the longest-term unemployed, federal supplemental unemployment benefits - available after regular state jobless compensation is exhausted - protect against eviction from homes, hunger, and even the break-up of families. In September 1983 this supplemental federal UI program came up for renewal. Conservative Republicans led the fight against extending coverage to those unemployed the longest. A key vote came on Rep. Carroll Campbell's (R-S.C.) motion to recommit the bill in order to cut the maximum benefit from 16 weeks to only 12 weeks. The Campbell motion was rejected by the House by a lopsided 141-278 vote on Sept. 29. For recommittal - Wrong. Against recommittal - Right.

In September 1983 the federal program of supplemental unemployment compensation came up for renewal in the Congress. Republicans fought efforts to extend and strengthen the program's benefits to help the long-term jobless. The key fight in the Senate was whether the legislation should include up to eight weeks of benefits for those unemployed who had exhausted all compensation and were no longer receiving UI checks. Democrats in the House included this provision in the bill over strong Republican opposition (see House Vote 8). Under increasing pressure from President Reagan, the Republican-controlled Senate rejected an amendment by Sen. Robert Byrd (D-W.Va.) to add this "reachback" benefit to the bill. The Byrd amendment went down 37-54 on Sept. 30. Fortunately, later in conference the benefits were added to the final bill. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

Following rejection of the Byrd amendment (see Senate Vote 4) Sen. Carl Levin (D-Mich.) offered an amendment to add up to 10 weeks of benefits for jobless workers in states with the highest unemployment rates, and lesser amounts for those in states with lower jobless rates. Again Republicans objected to helping the jobless, and the Levin amendment was rejected 26-64 on Sept. 30. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

The unfairness of Reaganomics became apparent again in late 1983 when Congress considered a 4 percent pay raise that had been promised to federal civilian and military personnel. The Reagan tax cuts for the wealthy had pushed the budget deficit to $200 billion, and conservatives in Congress moved to reduce that deficit - not by restoring fair taxes on the wealthy, but by taking back a portion of the federal workers' pay raise before it even took effect. Rep. James Jones (D-Okla.) offered an amendment to delay the four percent raise by three months - in effect, giving federal workers only nine months of a raise instead of a full year. The Jones amendment was approved by a 245-176 vote on Oct. 25 despite the Presidential pay panel's recommendation of a 21.5 percent raise to make federal workers' pay comparable to that in the private sector for equivalent job skills. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

Late in 1982 Congress passed a highway improvements job-creation bill to help bring the nation out of the Reagan recession. This legislation is providing up to 400,000 man-years of work on much needed rehabilitation of highways and other public works. To make sure the funds would create the maximum number of jobs, Congress included strict "Buy American" provisions to guarantee use of American steel and other materials, not Japanese or other foreign products. In 1983 the Senate considered new legislation that would have weakened these Buy American protections, providing exemptions for contracts of less than $500,000 and reducing the Buy American requirement to only 51 percent of the cost of the project. These changes, for example, would have allowed the use of more than 550,000 tons of foreign steel, costing 3,700 jobs in the U.S. steel industry alone. Sen. Howard Metzenbaum (D-Ohio) offered an amendment to stop the weakening of the Buy American policy, but his amendment was killed by Sen. John Chafee's (R-R.I.) tabling motion, 55-35, on Oct. 25. Fortunately, the bill later failed to achieve final enactment, and the Buy American provisions of the highway jobs bill were left intact. For tabling - Wrong. Against tabling - Right.

The flood of imported goods has caused the decline of major U.S. industries and the loss of millions of American jobs. While our toughest trade competitors such as Japan vigorously promote and subsidize their industries and restrict imports, the Reagan Administration and its conservative allies in Congress insist on keeping the U.S. wide open to imported goods. Often U.S. products must compete with foreign goods produced with heavy government aid under low-wage conditions. In 1983 these one-way trade policies generated the worst trade deficit in manufactured goods in U.S. history, exploding to nearly $70 billion - double that of 1982. Every billion dollars in deficit translates into 25,000 to 50,000 lost job opportunities. To help reverse industrial decline, the AFL-CIO and its affiliates worked hard to achieve passage of the domestic auto content bill, which would require foreign auto and truck manufacturers with large sales volume in the United States to produce increasing portions of their vehicles here, using American labor and materials. This legislation would restore an estimated one million jobs in auto production and its supplier industries of steel, glass, electronics, rubber, textiles, plastics, etc. In a major victory for labor, the House approved the content bill by a 219-199 vote on Nov. 3. The legislation faces an uncertain future in the Senate where conservative Republicans are in control, and President Reagan has declared his opposition to the measure. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

corrections: bill from the roll call's own Voteview description (S. J. Res. 194); the bill_number field is empty
aflcio_description: Since 1981 federal government employees have been targeted by the Reagan Administration for massive layoffs, arbitrary cuts in pay, and reduction in job-related benefits. In 1983 conservatives in Congress found a new way to attack federal workers' collectively bargained job benefits: through legislation prohibiting use of federal funds on any health insurance program that includes abortion coverage. The AFL-CIO has taken no position on the issue of abortion; however, to the federation the key issue in this case was not abortion but whether Congress could disregard the limited collective bargaining rights of federal workers by terminating certain health benefits which they had won and which are available to private-sector employees. Arch-conservative Sen. Jeremiah Denton (R-Ala.) led the charge against federal employees with an amendment which would have stopped funding for federal workers' health insurance. Sen. Lowell Weicker (R-Conn.) moved to kill the Denton amendment, but failed in a 44-51 vote on Nov. 9. For tabling - Right. Against tabling - Wrong.

bill_title: Affordable Telephone Service for All Consumers
aflcio_description: Under a federal court order, the American Telephone & Telegraph Co. was broken up on Jan. 1, 1984, into seven regional companies that provide local service. A new AT&T keeps long-distance lines and other operations. The shake-up of the nation's telephone system threatens to double or even triple phone rates for basic residential service. While proposed local rate increases are state regulatory matters that Congress cannot prevent, proposals for nationwide rate increases did come under congressional scrutiny in 1983. These were the proposed "access charges" that the pro-business Federal Communications Commission (FCC) sought to allow AT&T to impose for access to long-distance lines. Residential consumers would be hit with extra charges beginning at $2 per month in 1984 and increasing to as much as $10 per month in 1990 - even if the consumer made no long-distance calls. And this would be on top of state-approved rate increases. Most of this money would be soaked up by AT&T as extra profits. The AFL-CIO urged Congress to prohibit the access charge, warning that a combination of rate increases could make basic telephone service unaffordable for many Americans, especially the poor and elderly on fixed incomes. The House passed legislation to ban the access charges, with a key vote coming on an amendment by Rep. Tom Tauke (R-Iowa) which would have merely delayed the charges until a later date. The Tauke amendment was rejected 142-264 on Nov. 10. President Reagan has indicated he opposes legislation to prevent the unfair access charges. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

The AFL-CIO has long supported the Equal Rights Amendment, which states simply that "Equality of rights under the law shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or by any State on account of sex." The American public supports ERA by a 2-to-1 margin, but it has become the target of right-wing extremists. Although ERA passed the Congress in 1972 and was subsequently ratified by 35 states, right-wing efforts were successful in blocking ratification by the three additional state legislatures needed to make it part of the U.S. Constitution by the June 1982 deadline. In 1983, the AFL-CIO joined with women's and civil rights organizations in a new campaign to gain adoption of ERA. Although approved quickly by House committee, the amendment temporarily ran aground during a procedural squabble in the House. By a close 278-147 House vote on Nov. 15, the House failed to approve ERA. This was six votes short of the two-thirds majority needed to pass a Constitutional amendment under the expedited debate procedure backed by ERA proponents. House Floor action on ERA is expected again in 1984. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

bill_title: Preventing Further Hikes in Home Heating Bills
aflcio_description: President Reagan signaled his national energy policy shortly after his inauguration when he removed all remaining federal price controls on domestically produced oil. As a result the pump price of gasoline, an oil by-product, immediately jumped 8-10 cents per gallon. Since then Reagan has tried to remove the remaining price controls on natural gas prices. Since Congress partially deregulated natural gas in 1978, prices have skyrocketed. During the 1982-83 winter alone, residential price increases averaged 25 percent across the country, with some regions facing boosts as large as 60 percent. More than 300,000 families spent last winter without heat because they couldn't afford to pay sky-high fuel bills. In the Senate, conservatives led the fight for the big companies. Sen. James McClure (R-Ida.) offered legislation to give the oil companies who control natural gas production another $40 billion windfall in higher gas prices. Fortunately, most Senators realized that Americans are fed up with oil company rip-offs, and rejected the McClure amendment 28-67 on Nov. 15. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

bill_title: Maintaining a Strong Public School System
corrections: printed marker 'For - Wrong' contradicts the AFL-CIO's own roster grid on p6, which scores a Yea on this roll call as Right for all 8 senators tested; position set to Y. Roll 355 is the motion to table the Dole amendment, which the AFL-CIO opposed; bill from the roll call's own Voteview description (H. J. Res. 290); the bill_number field is empty
aflcio_description: Reagan Administration cuts in federal funds for education have forced local school districts to eliminate many worthwhile teaching programs. Despite this, the President led the charge in 1983 for special tax credits for those who send their children to private schools. The AFL-CIO opposes tuition tax credits on the grounds that they would weaken the nation's public school system. Furthermore, the Reagan-backed legislation would cost the Treasury close to $800 million per year, increasing pressure to cut programs in public education. Sen. Robert Dole (R-Kans.) offered the Reagan tuition tax credit scheme on Nov. 16. The Senate responded to the Administration's proposal for an additional tax loss in a time of $200 billion budget deficits and killed the Dole amendment 59-38. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

In 1983, Congress continued its struggle to restore an element of fairness in taxes, after it had approved in 1981 the largest tax giveaway in the nation's history. After extended discussions and maneuvering, the House fashioned a compromise tax bill which would have raised $8 billion in new revenues over three years through a variety of carefully constructed tax reforms. This bill would have closed some of the 1981 Reagan tax loopholes and solved a number of other longstanding problems in the tax code. The bill also contained a prohibition against taxation of employee fringe benefits - a new tax on working people that President Reagan had been pushing. Unfortunately, many of the same representatives who voted for the irresponsible Reagan tax windfalls voted to kill this tax reform bill by defeating the debate rule for consideration of the bill. The rule failed to achieve passage by a 204-214 vote on Nov. 17, thus preventing action on the tax bill. For the rule - Right. Against the rule - Wrong.

The National Institute for Occupational Safety & Health (NIOSH) is the government agency that provides health-related technical information to the Occupational Safety & Health Administration (OSHA) and to the Mine Safety & Health Administration (MSHA). For example, NIOSH recommends acceptable standards on workplace chemicals and tests and certifies protective equipment; OSHA and MSHA then set the standards and enforce them. Early in the Reagan Administration, Congress transferred NIOSH from Washington, D.C., to the Atlanta-based Centers for Disease Control. This was seen as an attempt to undercut NIOSH's mission by placing it at a geographical distance from OSHA and MSHA. In 1983 Rep. John Dingell (D-Mich.) offered an amendment to bring NIOSH under the jurisdiction of the Washington-based National Institutes of Health. The AFL-CIO argued that this would improve the efficiency of NIOSH and urged the House to approve the Dingell amendment. The proposal was defeated 186-206 on Nov. 17. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

As a result of the Communications Act of 1934 and subsequent regulatory action by the Federal Communications Commission, the government for the last five decades has pursued a policy of promoting reasonably priced, universal telephone service for all citizens. The result of this federal policy is that 92 percent of all Americans now have access to the nation's telephone system. This public policy was, however, jeopardized following the court-ordered breakup of American Telephone & Telegraph, which precipitated an anti-consumer regulatory ruling by the FCC, now under the conservative control of Reagan appointees. The FCC proposed to allow a flat charge on residential and small business phone users for the right of access to long-distance service whether they use such service or not. The fee originally was to go into effect in April of 1984, starting at $2 per month for residential customers and rising yearly until 1990. The AFL-CIO strongly opposed the access fee. Labor charged that the fee, when combined with increases in local rates, could raise local phone bills by as much as 100 percent, undermining the principle of universal telephone service. The AFL-CIO also pointed out the unfairness of a proposal which would penalize the 17 percent of all telephone customers who make no long-distance calls. In the Senate the key vote came on a bill sponsored by Sen. Robert Packwood (R-Ore.) that would have temporarily banned FCC imposition of the access fee. The bill also included an important pension rights plan that would allow employees of the new telephone companies created under divestiture to transfer their pension rights to their new employers. However, one day before the vote, the FCC announced that it was postponing implementation until at least June of 1985. The FCC counter-move clearly undercut Packwood's effort as the Senate, by a 44-40 vote on Jan. 26, agreed to a motion by Sen. Barry Goldwater (R-Ariz.) to table consideration of the Packwood bill. (The pension protection provision was later included in an unrelated tax bill which was signed into law.) For tabling - Wrong. Against tabling - Right.

bill_title: Corporate Abuse of Bankruptcy Law Threatened to Destroy Worker Benefits
aflcio_description: A serious threat to every protection in the union contracts of American workers arose in 1984. Following the example of Continental Airlines, company after company used the bankruptcy law to oust their employees' unions and arbitrarily shred collective bargaining agreements, fire workers, alter work rules, and reduce pay and pension benefits. This union-busting misuse of federal bankruptcy law was sanctioned in February by the U.S. Supreme Court's Bildisco decision. If left intact, this ruling threatened to render worthless the nation's long-standing system of collective bargaining and to undermine union-won benefits like health care, pensions, seniority and work rules. On the day the court handed down its ruling, the AFL-CIO went to work in Congress to reverse it. The AFL-CIO sought legislation to require a company in financial distress first to obtain the permission of a bankruptcy court before it could modify or reject its collective bargaining agreement. Then, if the company was found to be truly in financial distress, it would have to engage in collective bargaining to reduce pay and benefits only to the extent necessary to save the company. In the process, the company would have to open its books to the workers' representatives, and management would have to assume its share of pay and benefit cuts. An overwhelming bipartisan majority in both the House and Senate agreed with labor's position. In the House, the collective bargaining protection provision was included as part of a larger omnibus bankruptcy bill. When the bill reached the House floor, the key vote came on the procedural question of the debate rule under which the bill would be considered by the full House. The rule was limited so as to allow only specific amendments. Conservative Republicans, backed by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and others in the business lobby, attempted to defeat the debate rule in order to get at the collective bargaining safeguard. Their effort was resoundingly defeated by a 242-166 vote on Mar. 21. Later, Congress approved the bankruptcy bill and it was signed into law. The new law not only nullifies the Supreme Court's Bildisco decision and puts a stop to corporate abuse of federal bankruptcy law, but also safeguards the integrity of union contracts by compelling employers to engage in good-faith bargaining over any contract changes necessary to allow the firm to reorganize to stay in business. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

corrections: date 1984-04-06 -> 1984-04-10 per Voteview roll 432; no Senate roll call was cast on 6 April
aflcio_description: In 1981 the AFL-CIO and other organizations predicted that the Reagan tax cuts, which included steep reductions in the taxes paid by the wealthy and corporations, would hemorrhage the federal treasury at a cost of hundreds of billions of dollars in lost revenues. By 1984 this prediction had come true as the nation staggered toward a $200 billion Reagan budget deficit - more than the total accumulated deficits of every president from George Washington through Jimmy Carter. As deficits mounted, the AFL-CIO proposed a range of tax reforms designed to get the deficit under control. One of them - a $700 cap on the individual tax cuts - would have retained the full tax break for those earning $45,000 or less but limited the tax windfall for the rich to $700. Unfortunately, in June 1983, the Senate rejected this key tax reform. During Senate debate this year on a bill designed to reduce the deficit, Sen. John Chafee (R-R.I.) offered another labor-backed reform amendment - postponing for three years the indexation of the tax system Congress enacted as part of the Reagan tax program. The Chafee amendment would have raised $15 billion over the three-year period, mostly from the wealthy. Choosing to ignore its revenue impact, the Senate by a 57-38 vote on Apr. 6 agreed to a motion by Sen. Robert Dole (R-Kans.), chairman of the Senate Finance Committee, to table and thus kill the Chafee amendment. For tabling - Wrong. Against tabling - Right.

bill_title: Restoring Health Insurance for the Unemployed
aflcio_description: One of the important recession relief programs pushed by the AFL-CIO was legislation to provide health care benefits for the unemployed. When workers are jobless they usually lose health care insurance. Since most jobless workers are unable to pay the costly premiums for private insurance and are not eligible for Medicaid, they and their families must do without basic medical care. With more than eight million persons jobless for much of 1984, the AFL-CIO continued to push for a program of health care for the unemployed. During debate on a tax increase bill, Sen. John Heinz (R-Pa.) offered an amendment to make $700 million in federal grants available to the states to provide health care benefits to the long-term unemployed. As it did in 1983, the conservative-controlled Senate rejected this amendment by a 39-57 vote on Apr. 11. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

The corporate share of tax revenues to operate the federal government has fallen from 25 percent in 1960 to 6.6 percent in 1983. Individuals - mostly working families - have had to make up the difference. The largest plunge in big-business tax contributions to the federal government came as a result of the 1981 Reagan tax bill, which cut the effective corporate income tax rate in half at a loss of $170 billion over five years. The corporate tax system is so lopsided now that in 1984, about 90,000 corporations will pay no taxes. Most firms in the chemical industry, for example, not only did not pay taxes in 1983, but received $211 million in refunds or write-offs to reduce future taxes. To correct this gross inequity, Senators Howard Metzenbaum (D-Ohio) and Edward Kennedy (D-Mass.) during debate on a miscellaneous tax bill offered an amendment to impose a minimal 15 percent tax on corporate profits in excess of $50,000. The amendment was designed to restore a small measure of fairness and raise $19.1 billion over a five-year period. Despite the fact that the nation faced a staggering $200 billion deficit, the amendment was rejected by a 62-30 vote on a tabling motion by Finance Committee Chairman Robert Dole (R-Kans.) on Apr. 12. For tabling - Wrong. Against tabling - Right.

bill_title: Failure to Win Tax Relief for Construction Workers
aflcio_description: In 1984 the AFL-CIO backed legislation to permit construction workers to deduct their ordinary and necessary business expenses from their income taxes, just as other taxpayers already do. This tax adjustment was necessary because, under current law, the constraints and limitations on travel and business expenses do not adequately reflect the unique circumstances in the construction trades. As a result, many workers are unfairly treated. Today's construction workers are frequently employed on sites that are far from home. Under current federal income tax law, traveling expenses (including meals and lodging) are deductible if they are incurred while away from home in the pursuit of a trade or business. But such employment must be temporary and expected to last a short period of time. Traveling expenses incurred in connection with employment that is considered to be of indefinite or indeterminate duration generally are not tax deductible. But in the real world of construction, job-related travel expenses do not lend themselves to the distinction between temporary and indefinite employment. Thus, there is uncertainty and inequity in denying these workers an income tax deduction for legitimate costs associated with their jobs. During Senate debate on a miscellaneous tax bill, Sen. John Melcher (D-Mont.) offered an amendment to incorporate this long overdue tax clarification. Senate Finance Committee Chairman Sen. Robert Dole (R-Kans.) successfully killed the Melcher proposal, tabling it by a 50-31 vote on Apr. 12. For tabling - Wrong. Against tabling - Right.

bill_title: Increasing Senior Citizen Health Care Costs - I
corrections: no date printed on the scorecard; 1984-05-09 per Voteview roll 461
aflcio_description: No sooner had the Senate rejected the revenue-raising curb on indexing (see Senate vote #4), than it voted for an increase in Medicare costs for the elderly as a way to reduce the federal budget deficit. At present senior citizens and disabled Medicare beneficiaries spend an average of 20 percent of their limited incomes on medical care. The tax bill reported by the Senate Finance Committee would have compounded this financial burden by increasing the Part B Medicare premium and by raising the Medicare deductible. Part B is a medical insurance program that pays up to 80 percent of the reasonable charges for a range of elderly health care services, including doctor and outpatient hospital care, outpatient physical therapy and home health care. The AFL-CIO charged that if medical care costs continued to rise at the present pace, which is greater than the inflation rate in the rest of the economy, monthly medicare premiums would also increase at rates far exceeding the annual cost-of-living adjustments for social security benefits. It was further estimated that if the Finance Committee bill passed, premium increases by 1990 could consume 30 percent of this annual cost-of-living increase. During debate on the tax increase package, Sen. Edward M. Kennedy (D-Mass.) offered an amendment to eliminate the increase in the Part B premium. The conservative-controlled Senate, however, rejected the Kennedy amendment and thereby voted for the Medicare increases when it agreed by a 58-36 vote to a tabling motion by Sen. Robert Dole (R-Kans.). For tabling - Wrong. Against tabling - Right.

bill_title: Increasing Senior Citizen Health Care Costs - II
corrections: tally printed prevailing-side-first as 50-44; the roll call is 44-50 per Voteview roll 468
aflcio_description: After the defeat of the Kennedy Medicare amendment, Sen. Max Baucus (D-Mont.) countered with an amendment designed to restore $588 million of the total $9 billion in Medicare cuts proposed by the Senate Finance Committee. The Baucus amendment would have eliminated the proposed increase in the Medicare Part B deductible and reduced the Part B premium increases in 1987 so that premium hikes would not exceed the rate of inflation. It would have also provided for closer monitoring of physician behavior under the proposed physician fee freeze so that Medicare beneficiaries could be protected from unfair cost shifting during the two-year freeze. During debate, Sen. Baucus pointed out that of the $9 billion in Medicare costs, senior citizens were required to contribute $3.7 billion in higher medical fees while physicians and hospitals were only required to make up $2.9 billion through reduced fees. Once again the fiscal conservatives turned their backs on senior citizens and voted down the Baucus amendment by a 50-44 vote on May 17. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

Sen. Jesse Helms (R-N.C.), whose 1984 re-election campaign is expected to set a spending record of $20 million, attempted to legislate a sweeping attack on the political spending rights of unions. The Helms amendment would have prohibited unions from using dues money for educational activities, such as voter registration, get-out-the-vote drives and political communications to union members. He would have denied unions the right to finance the cost of political action committees, a right now granted under federal election law to both unions and corporations. The broad reach of the Helms amendment would have applied to both federal and state elections. Further, despite the fact that federal election law treats union and corporate activity equally, the Helms amendment would not have limited in any way the right of corporations to spend their treasury funds for the same activities. The obvious purpose of the Helms amendment was to restrict the right of unions to exercise their First-Amendment right to communicate with their members on political issues, prevent unions from encouraging their members to participate in the democratic election process, interfere in unprecedented fashion with the right of states to enact their own campaign finance rules, and destroy the neutrality of the federal election act with regard to corporate and union treasury spending in federal elections. Realizing that the Helms amendment was nothing more than an anti-union attack promoted by the National Right to Work Committee, the Senate again rejected the Helms amendment as it had done in 1982. But this time it was rejected by an even larger margin. On May 22, the Senate voted 65-32 for a motion by Sen. Charles Mathias (R-Md.) to table and thus kill the Helms amendment. For tabling - Right. Against tabling - Wrong.

bill_title: Protecting U.S. Jobs from Illegal Immigration
aflcio_description: The AFL-CIO has long opposed the heavy flow of illegal immigration, which not only undercuts job opportunities for unemployed Americans but undermines U.S. labor standards as well. Illegal aliens, meanwhile, are often the victims of the worst kinds of worker exploitation. To stop the flow of illegal aliens, the primary solution is to remove the lure of employment opportunity, and the only way to accomplish that is to impose tough penalties on employers who hire persons unauthorized to work in the United States. In 1984, the AFL-CIO pushed for enactment in the omnibus immigration bill of tough penalties against employers who knowingly hire illegal aliens. While the original legislation contained such penalties, the bill that emerged from the House Judiciary Committee had been substantially weakened. For example, the committee bill failed to require an employer to check the documentation of those hired unless the employer had been notified previously by the Attorney General that it had hired an undocumented alien in its workforce. This would make it nearly impossible to prove that an employer had "knowingly" employed an illegal alien. Further injunctions against employers violating the law were reserved only for special circumstances rather than being a standard remedy for every violation. Finally, the enforcement process itself was so elaborate and time-consuming that a scofflaw employer could stave off any penalty for years. As a result, when the bill came to the House floor the AFL-CIO backed an amendment by Rep. Gus Hawkins (D-Calif.) to remedy several of the shortcomings. The responsibility for checking a worker's identification was clearly made the duty of the employer. Injunctions were made standard in all cases, and a court procedure was established to expedite the enforcement process. The Hawkins proposal went even further by outlawing discrimination in hiring, screening or referring on the basis of a citizen's or legal resident alien's national origin or status. Despite these improvements, the House rejected the Hawkins amendment by a 166-253 vote on June 12. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

bill_title: Setting Labor Standards for Foreign Workers
aflcio_description: Another issue of longstanding concern to the AFL-CIO has been the misuse of the existing "H-2" temporary foreign worker program. This program now allows employers to use temporary foreign workers so long as, in the words of the existing law, "unemployed persons capable of performing such service or labor cannot be found in this country." While complaints about the program abound, since H-2 is administered by the Dept. of Labor, it has remained relatively small in size and protective of the rights of both domestic workers who have priority for the jobs and those foreign workers whose admission has been authorized. Once again, however, the Judiciary Committee weakened the existing H-2 limitations. The committee bill specifically eliminated the language protecting the pre-emptive employment right of jobless U.S. workers. It also weakened administrative oversight for H-2 by assigning approval of its regulations to the Attorney General with a significant role to be played by the Secretary of Agriculture. During debate Rep. George Miller (D-Calif.) offered an amendment that would have: (1) maintained the H-2 program as is; (2) tightened restrictions by insuring that non-agricultural H-2 workers would be admitted only if there were not enough qualified workers available here to perform the work in question and then only if the employment of these workers would not adversely affect American wages and working conditions; and (3) establish a commission to review the H-2 program. Despite strong labor support for the Miller amendment, the House rejected it by a 164-256 vote on June 14. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

bill_title: Bracero Program - Importing More Foreign Workers
aflcio_description: After rejecting amendments to strengthen the immigration bill with respect to limitations on foreign workers, the House turned around and approved an amendment by Rep. Leon Panetta (D-Calif.) to re-establish the discredited "bracero" program. This program, which was killed by Congress in 1964, had permitted the importation of hundreds of thousands of foreign agricultural workers who displaced U.S. farm and migrant workers and undercut American working standards. Bracero workers were subjected to some of the worst cases of exploitation in our nation's history. These abuses were recorded in an award-winning expose by the late Edward R. Murrow in the famous television documentary film, "Harvest of Shame." Under the Panetta amendment, not only would the bracero program be given new life, but no termination date was set for it. Unlimited numbers of foreign workers would be admitted into the U.S. to do agricultural work. No government determination would be required to certify that there were insufficient domestic workers available to do the work, and few protections would be provided foreign workers coming into the United States. Despite strong opposition by labor, Hispanic, church and public interest groups, the House approved the Panetta amendment by a 228-172 vote on June 14. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

aflcio_description: Although the AFL-CIO had maintained a strong commitment to support immigration legislation in 1984, the rejection of both the Hawkins and Miller amendments, followed by the adoption of the Panetta bracero amendment, forced the AFL-CIO to oppose the final House version of the immigration bill. Despite this [...] approved by a narrow 216-211 [...] [Against] - Right.

bill_title: Working Women - Child Day Care Services
corrections: no date printed on the scorecard; 1984-06-27 per Voteview roll 533
aflcio_description: With working women and single-parent households comprising an ever-larger proportion of the U.S. labor force, one of their most pressing needs is for affordable and adequate child day care services. In the absence of a comprehensive child day care program, many women have already had to abandon their jobs and turn to welfare. For others, turning their children into "latchkey kids" is the only alternative. The AFL-CIO has long been on record in support of federal assistance to establish programs providing infant care, kindergarten and after-school child day care services at affordable rates. During Senate debate on legislation designed to upgrade mathematics and science education in the nation's schools, Sen. Don Riegle (D-Mich.) offered an amendment to provide $15 million in seed money over the next three years to establish after-school day care programs using existing school facilities. Although a similar bill had been unanimously passed by the House, Senate conservatives voted 51-42 in support of a motion by Sen. Howard Baker (R-Tenn.) to kill the amendment. For tabling - Wrong. Against tabling - Right.

Voteview tags this roll call 'HR5172', which occurs exactly once in the whole 98th Senate and sits inside a run of nine H.R. 5712 roll calls on the same bill and day (rolls 550-559); corrected to H.R. 5712. aflcio_description: In 1983 Congress authorized the creation of the National Endowment for Democracy, a federally financed, private non-profit organization whose various activities, such as fostering trade unions in developing countries, are designed to promote the [...] of democratic institutions abroad. The AFL-CIO through its Free Trade Union Institute is a participating organization in the Endowment program. When the 1985 funding authorization for the Endowment reached Congress, it immediately came under attack in the House where the entire $31 million appropriation was deleted. (See House Vote #13.) In the Senate several attempts were made to slash the Endowment's funds. While more drastic amendments to eliminate all funding were rejected, Sen. aflcio_description: Since the energy crisis of the 1970s, the AFL-CIO has vigorously supported federal policies and legislative remedies aimed at achieving energy independence through prudent energy development, conservation and alternative energy sources. Synthetic fuels are substitutes for natural gas or petroleum that are made from coal, shale, tar sands and hydrogen from water. Recognizing the contribution that these activities make to the evolution of democracy abroad, the Congress in 1983 authorized creation of the National Endowment for Democracy. The Endowment is a federally financed, private, non-profit organization whose various activities, such as fostering trade unions in developing countries, are designed to promote democratic institutions. The AFL-CIO, through its Free Trade Union Institute (FTUI), is a participating organization in the Endowment program. bill_title: Environmental Protection for Workers and Families
aflcio_description: In 1980 Congress recognized that abandoned toxic waste dumps are a major environmental and health hazard. Unfortunately, the 1980 legislation failed to include a key provision for victim compensation which had been opposed by Senate Republicans. Now, under the Reagan Administration, the "superfund" clean-up plan has been slowed to a crawl. A major scandal in 1983 over "superfund" mismanagement resulted in massive resignations of the Reagan-appointed EPA hierarchy. In 1984, Congress considered a five-year reauthorization of the "superfund." The House version again included a key victim-compensation program. A study commissioned by the original 1980 clean-up law found that legal remedies available in state courts to victims of toxic waste were inadequate. The 1984 bill remedied this by permitting citizens to sue in federal court to gain compensation from companies for injuries caused by hazardous wastes, to force actions to clean up a site if the EPA or the states have not taken such action, or to make EPA carry out the provisions of the superfund law. Once again conservatives led the fight to strike down the victim-compensation provision as they had done in 1980. Despite labor's opposition, the House by a narrow 208-200 vote on Aug. 9 approved an amendment by conservative Rep. Harold Sawyer (R-Mich.) to delete the legal rights provision for toxic waste victims. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

aflcio_description: In early 1984 the U.S. Supreme Court handed down a regressive ruling that undermined federal civil rights law, overturning a lower court decision which had found sex discrimination at Grove City College in Pennsylvania. The court's conservative majority narrowly constricted the provisions of Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972 which barred sex discrimination in any educational "program or activity receiving federal financial assistance." Although Grove City College is a recipient of federal financial assistance, the court majority defined Title IX's "program or activity" language so narrowly as to reach only the school's student financial aid program, rather than the entire school as the lower court had held. The result of the decision was to undermine the federal law's comprehensive prohibition against sex discrimination in education. Not surprisingly, in keeping with the Reagan Administration's abysmal civil rights record, the Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights stated publicly that he would seek to broaden the reach of the Grove City ruling by applying it to other civil rights laws. The AFL-CIO and the Leadership Conference on Civil Rights almost immediately countered with legislation to reverse Grove City. It would restore to four key civil rights statutes the broad scope and coverage that was originally intended by Congress and enforced by the federal government for the last 20 years. While the bill easily passed the House with strong bipartisan support, Senate Republicans blocked action. The chief opponent was Labor Committee Chairman Orrin Hatch (R-Utah), who bottled up the labor-backed bill in his committee. A last-ditch attempt by Sen. Robert Byrd (D-W.Va.) to add the Grove City repealer bill to an unrelated continuing appropriations bill failed in the waning hours of the 98th Congress. When it was clear that opponents would be successful in killing the civil rights measure, the bill's original cosponsor Sen. Robert Packwood (R-Ore.) moved to table his own amendment as a means to secure a recorded vote on the issue. His amendment was tabled by a 53-45 vote on Oct. 2. For tabling - Wrong. Against tabling - Right.

Besides record budget deficits, the Reagan Administration's "do-nothing" trade policies bear direct responsibility for a record U.S. trade deficit - projected to be a staggering $125 billion in 1985. This translates into a loss of three million American jobs. Since Reagan took office, the deficit in manufactured goods alone has gone from a $5.3 billion surplus to an $85 billion deficit. While these deficits mounted, the U.S. steel industry continued to be ransacked by foreign imports whose cheaper prices were sustained by a laundry list of unfair trade practices by the exporting countries. Because of this, steel imports captured a record 33 percent of the U.S. market, and steel employment fell to less than 60 percent of 1979 levels. To stop this economic plunder, the U.S. International Trade Commission - the agency charged with investigating unfair trade practices - recommended quotas and tariffs on imports to help the ailing steel industry. But President Reagan refused to implement these remedies and instead announced he would seek to negotiate "voluntary" import restraints with exporters. Congress found his response insufficient. On Oct. 3 the House, by an overwhelming 285-134 vote, approved legislation giving the President stronger enforcement powers against unfair steel imports and calling on him to reduce these imports to 17 percent of the U.S. market. For - Right. Against - Wrong.
